entry.title: Managing Multiple Brands in SAP SuccessFactors Recruiting Marketing (RMK)
entry.content:
Introduction

As organizations expand across different businesses, subsidiaries, and geographical locations, maintaining a single employer brand may not always meet their recruitment requirements. Each business may have its own identity, target audience, recruitment strategy, and career opportunities.

Consider an organization operating two different brands. One focuses on industrial and operational recruitment, while the other primarily recruits for technology and corporate positions.

Although both businesses use the same SAP SuccessFactors Recruiting landscape, they want candidates to experience their respective brands independently.

At first, the requirement may sound simple: create separate career homepages with different logos, colors, and content.

However, as we move further into the configuration, several questions arise.

How do we associate jobs with the appropriate brands? How can we ensure that candidates see only the jobs belonging to the brand they are visiting? How do Recruiting Management microsites and themes fit into the process? And what happens when each brand requires a different custom domain and SSL certificate?

In this blog, I'll walk through the different configurations involved in managing multiple brands using SAP SuccessFactors Recruiting Marketing (RMK) and Recruiting Management (RCM).

I'll also discuss practical implementation considerations, commonly encountered challenges, and areas worth validating before moving the career sites into production.

The examples mainly focus on environments using the Unified Data Model (UDM). Some configuration options and navigation paths may differ in legacy implementations.

Step 1: Creating Marketing Brands in Career Site Builder

The first step is establishing the employer brands that will be maintained within Career Site Builder.

SAP SuccessFactors Recruiting Marketing allows multiple brands to be configured within the same career site environment. Each brand can have its own visual identity, content, and candidate-facing experience.

To get started, navigate to Career Site Builder → Tools → Brand Management.

Here, we can create and maintain the employer brands required for the career site.

For example, an organization might have an existing Default Brand and want to introduce an additional employer brand, which we'll refer to as Brand B.

When creating a brand, pay attention to the brand name and URL Brand Identifier.

The URL Brand Identifier helps Career Site Builder distinguish the respective branded experience.

A consistent naming convention is useful because the brand information must later be connected with Recruiting Management.

One important point is that creating a brand does not automatically assign job requisitions to it. That association requires additional configuration.

Step 2: Creating Separate Homepages for Each Brand

Once the brands are configured, the next step is creating their individual career homepages.

Navigate to Career Site Builder → Pages → Home.

Select the relevant brand and locale, then configure its homepage.

Each brand can have different content, imagery, messaging, and navigation components.

For example, one brand may want to highlight operational excellence and engineering opportunities, while another may focus on workplace culture and technology careers.

Career Site Builder provides reusable components that can be arranged according to the brand's requirements.

An existing homepage can also serve as a starting point for another brand, provided any copied links, images, and content are reviewed carefully.

Creating separate homepages is useful, but the candidate experience should extend beyond the visual appearance.

Candidates must also be able to navigate easily and find the opportunities relevant to the brand they are exploring.

Step 3: Configuring Brand-Specific Global Styles

After creating the homepages, we can configure the visual identity of each brand.

Career Site Builder allows separate brands to maintain supported styling properties such as fonts, text colors, backgrounds, and buttons.

Navigate to Career Site Builder → Appearance → Styles → Global Styles.

Select the appropriate brand and maintain its styling.

This allows multiple brands to have distinct visual identities even when they share the same Recruiting Marketing environment.

Configuring separate headers and footers

Headers play an important role in maintaining a consistent brand experience across career site pages.

Navigate to Career Site Builder → Appearance → Styles → Headers.

Select the relevant brand and locale.

Each brand can have its own logo and supported navigation configuration.

For example, one brand might include links to Home, About Us, Locations, and Search Jobs, while another uses Home, Life at Our Company, Early Careers, and Search Jobs.

Similar considerations apply to footers, where organizations may maintain separate contact information, social media links, or other relevant content.

Understanding Job Layout styling

One area worth testing carefully is the job description page.

Sometimes a brand homepage displays the correct colors, but the job description page appears different.

To review the job layout, navigate to Career Site Builder → Layouts → Job Layouts.

The Job Layout editor provides supported configuration options and certain styling overrides, such as Apply Now button colors.

However, these options do not necessarily control every element of the job description page.

Formatting included in the External Job Description in Recruiting Management may also influence how the content appears.

I recommend checking both the Career Site Builder preview and the actual published job description page when validating brand styling.

Step 4: Configuring the Required Permissions

Before configuring the Recruiting Management integration, the relevant permissions should be reviewed.

Navigate to Admin Center → Manage Permission Roles.

Open the appropriate administrator role and review Administrator Permissions → Manage MDF Recruiting Objects → MarketingBrand.

Depending on the user's responsibilities, permissions such as View, Edit, Import, and Export may be required.

Administrators who maintain Marketing Brand objects may require editing permissions, while recruiters may only need the relevant field permissions to select the correct brand on their requisitions.

Career Site Builder administration permissions and job requisition template permissions should also be considered.

Step 5: Associating Marketing Brands with Job Requisitions

Creating a brand homepage does not automatically determine which jobs belong to that brand.

Recruiting Management must provide the appropriate Marketing Brand information.

Marketing Brand field in UDM

For implementations using the Unified Data Model, SAP provides the standard Marketing Brand field.

Field ID: sfstd_marketingBrand_obj

Field Type: object

Object Type: MarketingBrand

This field references the standard MarketingBrand generic object.

Review the Job Requisition Template and ensure that the field is configured through the supported template configuration approach.

<field-definition id="sfstd_marketingBrand_obj" type="object" required="false"
                  custom="false" object-type="MarketingBrand">
    <field-label><![CDATA[Marketing Brand]]></field-label>
    <field-label lang="en_GB"><![CDATA[Marketing Brand]]></field-label>
    <field-label lang="en_US"><![CDATA[Marketing Brand]]></field-label>
    <field-description><![CDATA[Marketing Brand]]></field-description>
    <field-description lang="en_GB"><![CDATA[Marketing Brande]]></field-description>
    <field-description lang="en_US"><![CDATA[Marketing Brand]]></field-description>
</field-definition>

Maintaining Marketing Brand on requisitions

Once the field and permissions are configured, recruiters can maintain the relevant Marketing Brand on job requisitions.

For example, a requisition belonging to Brand B should carry the corresponding Marketing Brand value.

An important consideration is that the Default Brand designation in Career Site Builder and the Marketing Brand object maintained on a requisition are related but should not be assumed to be interchangeable.

A note on legacy integrations

In older RCM–RMK integrations, Brand could be mapped to a Recruiting Management field such as Company Code through Admin Center → Setup Recruiting Marketing Job Field Mapping.

With UDM, the standard Marketing Brand generic object is used for the relevant brand association.

Before making changes, it is important to understand whether the system uses legacy mapping or has already adopted UDM.

Step 6: Creating Recruiting Management Microsites

The next step is reviewing the Recruiting Management side of the candidate experience.

Career Site Builder manages the external career site, while Recruiting Management handles additional candidate functionality during the application process.

RCM microsites can help maintain the appropriate recruiting site context for different brands.

Navigate to Admin Center → Manage Recruiting Sites.

Here, additional external recruiting sites can be created where required.

For example, an organization may retain its existing Default Recruiting Site and create another microsite for Brand B.

Each microsite has its own identifier, which is later used when associating the RCM site with the corresponding RMK brand.

An RCM microsite should not be confused with an RMK homepage. The microsite provides the relevant Recruiting Management site context.

Step 7: Creating and Configuring Themes for Multiple Brands

Once the microsites are configured, the next step is maintaining the appropriate themes for each brand.

An important point to understand is that SAP SuccessFactors provides two different theme management areas relevant to this configuration.

Configuring Recruiting Site Themes

Navigate to Admin Center → Manage Recruiting Sites → Manage Themes.

Here, we can create and maintain themes for the Recruiting Management career sites.

A new theme can be created by copying an existing theme and updating its supported styling properties.

For example, separate themes can be maintained for the Default Recruiting Site and an additional brand's microsite.

Under Fine Tune → Career Navigation, supported navigation colors can be configured.

Once the theme is ready, use the Visible to setting to associate it with the appropriate Recruiting Management site.

For example:

Default Recruiting Site → Default Recruiting Site Theme

Brand B Microsite → Brand B Recruiting Site Theme

The theme marked as Default is used for sites that do not have a separately assigned theme.

Creating a Theme for RMK Brand Assignment

Apart from the Recruiting Site Themes, we also need to configure the theme that will be selected in RMK Brand Management.

Navigate to Admin Center → Manage Themes.

Here, we can create a custom theme by duplicating an existing theme and modifying the supported appearance settings.

For example, the organization may maintain a separate theme for Brand B while retaining the existing default theme.

Once the theme is created and saved, it becomes available for selection through the Theme Name dropdown in Career Site Builder's Brand Management, subject to the configuration available in the environment.

It is important not to confuse these configurations. Recruiting Site Themes are maintained through Manage Recruiting Sites, while the theme selected in RMK Brand Management is maintained through Admin Center → Manage Themes.

These settings are also separate from the Global Styles configured in Career Site Builder.

Step 8: Connecting the RCM Microsite and Theme to the RMK Brand

After creating the RCM microsite and maintaining the relevant themes, the next step is associating them with the corresponding RMK brand.

Navigate to Career Site Builder → Tools → Brand Management.

Open the required brand and select Edit.

In the Update Brand window, review the following fields:

Microsite ID: Enter the identifier of the corresponding Recruiting Management microsite created under Manage Recruiting Sites.

Theme Name: Select the appropriate theme configured under Admin Center → Manage Themes.

For example, an organization may configure:

RMK Brand RCM Microsite Theme Name

Default BrandDefault Recruiting SiteDefault Theme
Brand BBrand B MicrositeBrand B Theme

These are illustrative values; the actual microsite IDs and theme names depend on the configuration.

Once the values are maintained, save the brand configuration.

An incorrect Microsite ID can cause application errors when candidates select Apply Now. Similarly, selecting the wrong Theme Name may result in an inconsistent appearance in the corresponding candidate experience.

After saving, test the candidate journey from the branded RMK homepage through the job description and application process.

The key distinction is that the Microsite ID connects the RMK brand to its RCM recruiting site, while the Theme Name selects the corresponding SAP SuccessFactors theme for that brand. Both should be validated separately to ensure a consistent candidate experience.

Step 9: Configuring Brand-Specific Job Search

Once the Marketing Brand and requisition configuration are complete, the next requirement is controlling which jobs appear in each brand's search results.

For UDM-enabled environments, navigate to Career Site Builder → Layouts → Search Results → Settings → General.

Two settings are especially important.

Enable Branded Search Form

When enabled, searches initiated from branded pages submit to the corresponding branded search results page.

Enable Branded Search Results

When enabled, results are restricted to jobs associated with the relevant brand.

With the appropriate configuration, candidates visiting Brand B's homepage should be able to search for opportunities associated with Brand B.

It is important to remember that branded search relies on the correct Marketing Brand information being maintained on the requisition.

What about the Default Brand?

The default search experience requires separate consideration.

An organization should not automatically assume that the Default Brand's main search results exclude jobs belonging to other brands.

If strict separation is required, the supported search and filtering behavior must be validated.

If a manually configured Search Jobs button is used, its destination should also be checked.

Step 10: Creating and Configuring Category Pages for Different Brands

Category Pages are another useful feature in Career Site Builder, allowing organizations to display specific job opportunities based on location, department, job category, or other supported requisition fields.

In a multi-brand implementation, category pages can be maintained separately for different brands and locales. This helps organizations provide more targeted job listings while maintaining the appropriate brand experience.

Creating a Category Page

To begin, navigate to Career Site Builder → Pages → Category.

Here, we can view the existing category pages along with their associated locales, brands, and statuses.

To create a new category page, select Add.

Enter a suitable category page name and select the appropriate Locale and Brand.

For example, an organization might create separate pages for Engineering Opportunities, Graduate Careers, or opportunities in a particular geographical region.

After saving, the page can be configured using the available components and Job List settings.

Configuring Job List Filters

Once the category page is created, open it and navigate to the Job List tab.

For UDM-enabled environments, Career Site Builder allows us to define the jobs displayed on a category page using keywords, locations, and additional field-based filters.

The Add Filter option allows administrators to select supported requisition fields and their corresponding values.

For example, suppose an organization wants to display only job opportunities located in Türkiye on a particular category page.

We can configure the following filter:

Field: Country/Region (jobLocationCountry)

Value: Türkiye

With this filter, the category page is configured to display jobs matching the selected Country/Region value.

Similarly, organizations can configure category pages using other supported fields and values based on their recruitment requirements.

Linking Category Pages to the Brand Homepage

Once the category page is configured and saved, it can be linked from the corresponding brand homepage.

For example, a homepage button such as Explore Opportunities can direct candidates to a category page containing relevant job listings.

This can be configured using supported homepage components or navigation links in Career Site Builder.

Important Consideration

It is important to understand that assigning a category page to a brand and filtering jobs by location are separate configurations.

Selecting a brand determines the brand and locale context of the category page, while Job List filters determine which opportunities are eligible to appear.

For example, assigning a category page to a particular brand does not automatically mean that every job matching its location filter has the correct Marketing Brand maintained in Recruiting Management.

For this reason, both the requisition's Marketing Brand assignment and the category page's Job List filters should be validated during testing.

This approach helps organizations create targeted job discovery experiences without relying solely on the main search results page.

Step 11: Configuring Brand-Specific Career Site URLs

Organizations may require separate career site URLs for different employer brands while continuing to use the same SAP SuccessFactors Recruiting Marketing environment.

For example:

Default Brand: careers.company.example

Brand B: careers.brandb.example

For UDM-enabled Career Site Builder environments, navigate to Career Site Builder → Brand Settings → Select Brand → Site URL.

Here, administrators can configure the brand's URL using the available options:

  • Custom Site URL: Uses an organization-owned domain and requires appropriate DNS and SSL configuration.

  • Standard Site URL: Uses an SAP-managed domain.

  • Path-Based Site URL: Allows access to the brand through a dedicated path under the existing career site domain.

Select the appropriate URL option and configure the Primary Site URL according to the organization's requirements.

When changing the primary URL, review the related job alert and email campaign settings, as these may also be affected.

For custom domains, ensure that the required DNS configuration and SSL certificate are in place, as discussed in the next step.

Note: Brand Settings is available for additional brands in UDM-enabled Career Site Builder environments. The Default Brand continues to use its existing site-level configuration.

Step 12: Managing SSL Certificates for Multiple Brand Domains

When an organization maintains multiple employer brands with separate custom domains, it is important to ensure that each domain is secured with a valid SSL certificate.

SSL certificates enable secure HTTPS communication between the candidate's browser and the career site.

In a multi-brand implementation, an organization may already have a working SSL certificate for its existing career site and need to configure another certificate for an additional brand.

To begin, navigate to Career Site Builder → Tools → SSL Certificates.

The SSL Certificates tool is available in the production environment and allows administrators to generate Certificate Signing Requests (CSRs), upload certificates, install them, monitor their validity, and manage renewals.

Understanding the SSL Certificate Installation Options

Career Site Builder provides two methods for obtaining and installing SSL certificates.

Option 1: Generate a CSR Through Career Site Builder

This is the typical approach when obtaining a new SSL certificate.

The process involves:

  1. Generate a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) in Career Site Builder.

  2. Submit the CSR to a trusted Certificate Authority.

  3. Obtain the signed SSL certificate.

  4. Submit the certificate through Career Site Builder.

  5. Install the certificate and verify its status.

When generating the CSR, maintain the appropriate domain and organization information.

The Common Name must correspond to the intended fully qualified hostname, without including the protocol or page path.

Career Site Builder generates and retains the corresponding private key for the CSR.

Option 2: Upload an SSL Certificate Obtained Externally

Organizations may also obtain SSL certificates using a CSR generated outside Career Site Builder.

In this scenario, use Option 2 → Upload SSL Certificate.

The upload dialog requires the signed SSL Certificate and its corresponding Private Key.

An Intermediate Certificate can also be uploaded when necessary.

The certificate files must be in a supported PEM format, using accepted extensions such as .CER, .CRT, or .PEM. Compressed ZIP files should be extracted before uploading.

Understanding Intermediate Certificates

Intermediate certificates establish the trust chain between the issued SSL certificate and the trusted Certificate Authority.

Depending on the certificate, Career Site Builder may retrieve the required intermediate certificate automatically.

However, if automatic retrieval is unsuccessful, the administrator may need to upload it manually.

Where multiple intermediate certificates are required, they may need to be combined into one supported certificate file.

This is an important consideration because an incomplete certificate chain can cause installation failures.

Verifying the Certificate Installation Status

After uploading and submitting the certificate, the installation request must be processed.

The SSL Certificates table provides information such as:

  • Reference ID

  • Common Name

  • Installation Status

  • Days to Expiry

  • Valid From and Valid To

  • Last Modified

  • Available Actions

Once the certificate is successfully installed, its status changes to Installed.

A certificate may also display an In Use indicator when it is actively associated with the career site.

The certificate's validity dates and remaining days before expiry help administrators plan renewals.

Troubleshooting SSL Installation Issues

A common issue occurs when an SSL certificate uploads successfully but later returns to Uninstalled.

SAP KBA 3298546 – SSL Installation in Uninstalled Status describes possible causes, including missing intermediate certificates, incomplete certificate chains, and certificate or private-key validation problems.

If the certificate status changes from Installation Requested to Uninstalled, review the installation audit history and verify the uploaded files.

Another possible scenario is a certificate remaining in Installation Requested status for an extended period.

SAP KBA 3375802 – SSL Stuck in Installation Requested Status explains when an installation that remains pending may require SAP Support investigation.

It is also worth reviewing certificate-authority-specific requirements. SAP KBA 3775701 – GoDaddy and Starfield SSL Certificate Issues documents additional intermediate-certificate considerations for certain GoDaddy and Starfield certificates.

Validating the Custom Domain

Once the SSL certificate is installed, verify that the brand-specific URL loads securely over HTTPS and displays the correct homepage.

Ensure that the DNS configuration points to the appropriate SAP RMK hosting destination without affecting existing brand configurations.

For more details, refer to SAP Help Portal – SSL Certificates Settings in Career Site Builder.

Step 13: Automating Marketing Brand Assignment Using Business Rules

In multi-brand implementations, organizations may want to automate Marketing Brand assignment rather than requiring recruiters to select the appropriate brand manually.

For example, the Marketing Brand can be determined based on the country, company, or other supported requisition attributes.

Example: Country-Based Marketing Brand Assignment

Consider an organization that wants to assign a specific Marketing Brand to requisitions created for a particular country, while all other requisitions use the Default Brand.

To configure the rule, navigate to Admin Center → Configure Business Rules.

In this example, the rule uses the following configuration:

  • Scenario: Configure Business Rules on Job Requisition

  • Job Requisition Template: Job Requisition (All)

  • Purpose: Save

The business rule evaluates the country associated with the requisition's company.

IF: Job Requisition Template → Company → Country equals the specified country.

THEN: Set Job Requisition Template → Brand to Brand B.

ELSE: Set Job Requisition Template → Brand to Default Brand.

This allows the Marketing Brand to be assigned according to the defined business requirement when the rule executes.

Assigning the Rule

After configuring the rule, navigate to Admin Center → Manage Rules in Recruiting and assign it to the appropriate job requisition template and trigger.

Troubleshooting and Common Challenges

While configuring multiple brands in SAP SuccessFactors Recruiting Marketing, certain issues may arise even when the initial setup appears correct. Here are three common challenges and their possible solutions.

1. Incorrect Branding on Job Description Pages

Issue: The career homepage displays the correct branding, but the job description page uses different colors or styles.

Resolution: Review Career Site Builder → Appearance → Styles → Global Styles and Layouts → Job Layouts. Also verify whether the External Job Description in RCM contains HTML formatting that overrides the expected styling.

2. Jobs From Other Brands Appear in Search Results

Issue: Candidates visiting one brand's career site can see job opportunities associated with another brand.

Resolution: Verify the Marketing Brand assigned to the requisition and review Career Site Builder → Layouts → Search Results → Settings → General.

Ensure that Enable Branded Search Form and Enable Branded Search Results are configured appropriately. The Default Brand's search behavior may differ from additional branded search pages.

3. Apply Now Redirects Incorrectly or Displays an Error

Issue: Candidates can view job descriptions but encounter an error or unexpected page when selecting Apply Now.

Resolution: Verify the microsite under Admin Center → Manage Recruiting Sites and compare its Microsite ID with the value maintained under Career Site Builder → Tools → Brand Management.

An incorrect microsite association can cause application redirection issues. Refer to SAP KBA 2829434 for further details.

Conclusion

Managing multiple brands in SAP SuccessFactors Recruiting Marketing goes beyond creating separate career homepages. It involves aligning Career Site Builder configurations, Marketing Brand assignments, RCM microsites, themes, branded job searches, and custom domains to deliver a consistent candidate experience.

With the right configuration and thorough testing, organizations can maintain distinct employer-brand identities while operating within a shared SAP SuccessFactors Recruiting environment.

Ultimately, the goal is to ensure that candidates experience the right brand, discover relevant opportunities, and enjoy a seamless journey from job search to application.

I hope this blog provides useful insights for anyone configuring or managing multiple brands in SAP SuccessFactors Recruiting Marketing.

entry.title: The "Project Cockpit" Request I've Heard in Almost Every SAP EPPM Engagement.
entry.content:
Introduction

For years, customers have asked for a simple way to navigate between Portfolio Items, PS Projects, PPM Projects, and CPM Projects without multiple clicks. In this blog, I share why SAP's new dashboard enhancement is more significant than it first appears and how it addresses a recurring challenge I have encountered across numerous SAP EPPM implementations.

The Reality of Working in an Integrated EPPM Landscape

Most organisations I have worked with don't use Portfolio Management in isolation.

A Portfolio Item is often just the starting point.

An idea is approved as a portfolio item, funding is allocated, and eventually execution objects are created. Depending on the organisation's processes, this may result in:

  • A PS Project for execution
  • A PPM Project for project management activities
  • A CPM Project for commercial project scenarios

From a system perspective, these relationships are established and available.

From a business user's perspective, however, understanding those relationships often required navigating through several screens.

And here's what I found interesting: users weren't asking for new functionality.

The relationships already existed.

The real ask was visibility.

They simply wanted to know:

  • Has the project been created?
  • Which project is linked?
  • Is something missing?
  • Can I jump directly to it?

A Requirement That Kept Reappearing

What is interesting is that this requirement has never been limited to a specific customer or industry.

Whether working with pharmaceutical organisations, manufacturing companies, engineering organisations, or capital project portfolios, the discussion was often the same:

"We need a cockpit view."

Customers wanted a single location where they could:

  • Validate project creation
  • Verify integration consistency
  • Navigate directly to related objects
  • Identify missing project relationships
  • Reduce navigation effort

But the underlying requirement was always the same:

"Give me one place where I can understand how everything is connected."

In fact, I've seen organisations invest considerable effort building custom reports, dashboard enhancements, and Fiori extensions specifically to provide this capability.

Not because the information wasn't available.

Simply because it wasn't available where users expected to find it.

Why the Recently Delivered SAP Note Caught My Attention

When I came across the SAP Note that enhances the Portfolio Item Dashboard with visibility of related objects and direct navigation capabilities, my immediate reaction was:

"Finally."

Not because it introduces a revolutionary new process.

Not because it changes how EPPM works.

But because it addresses a conversation that I have been having with customers for years.

The enhancement provides visibility of related project objects directly within the Portfolio Item Dashboard and allows users to navigate to them much more easily.

For many readers, that may sound like a small usability improvement.

For those of us who have spent years implementing EPPM, it feels like the delivery of a requirement that has existed for a very long time.

Why I Believe This Matters More Than the Feature Description Suggests

In my experience, user adoption is rarely driven by the most sophisticated functionality.

It is driven by how easy the system is to use every day.

The features users remember are often not the complex planning algorithms, financial calculations, or integration frameworks.

They remember the things that save them time.

They remember the frustrations that disappear.

That's why I believe this enhancement is more significant than it first appears.

It reduces unnecessary navigation.

It improves visibility.

It helps identify missing project relationships.

And perhaps most importantly, it gives users greater confidence in the data they are looking at.

How You Can Enable This in Your Landscape

If you're already using SAP EPPM and would like to take advantage of this enhancement, the good news is that the effort is relatively straightforward.

  • Implement the SAP Note

The first step is to implement SAP Note 3789571 - PPM-PFM: Enhancement portfolio item dashboard with all related objects (PPM/CPM/PS). This delivers the underlying functionality that exposes the related project objects within the Portfolio Item Dashboard.

  • Configure the Dashboard Fields

After implementing the note, you'll need to make the new fields available in the dashboard configuration.

SPRO Path:

SAP Portfolio and Project Management → Portfolio Management → Global Customizing → Global Field Settings → Dashboard Settings → Define Fields for Dashboards

Level

Behaviour

Per Dashboard Type

All dashboards of the same type share the same ALV personalization settings.

Per Context

More granular — personalization is defined per individual dashboard in the UI context. Context-level settings override Dashboard Type settings.

 

  • Consider Creating a Dedicated "Project Cockpit" View

While optional, I would strongly recommend creating a dedicated customer-specific dashboard view that surfaces the related project information prominently.

Conclusion

This enhancement addresses a practical SAP EPPM requirement I have seen repeatedly across customer implementations. Sometimes, relatively small usability improvements can make a significant difference to transparency, navigation and the overall user experience.

entry.title: SE16H Deep Dive for SAP Finance Joining BKPF, BSEG, and ACDOCA for Real-World Troubleshooting
entry.content:
Let us understand what this blog is about; SE16H is one of the most useful transaction in SAP for analyzing table data directly, especially when troubleshooting functional issues or validating document flows. Traditionally functional consultants used to download multiple tables on local machine and use excel for lookups and joins, compared to this SE16H is realtime flexible, and easy to use. Also it supports functions such as filtering, aggregation and join capabilities which makes functional consultants life easy. In this blog we will see in details how to use SE16H transaction with table join between BSEG, BKPF and ACDOCA. 

 

Learning Objectives

  • Understand what BKPF, BSEG, and ACDOCA represent in an S/4HANA Finance posting.
  • Build a reusable SE16H join definition with BSEG as the primary table and BKPF as a secondary table.
  • Extend the query with ACDOCA for document-level Universal Journal analysis.
  • Apply safe document-key join conditions and avoid joining on BELNR alone.
  • Use ledger and document filters to keep the query controlled and understandable.
  • Recognize why BSEG and ACDOCA do not always have a one-to-one line relationship.
  • Use the joined result to investigate profit center, cost center, G/L account, currency, and document-header context.
  • Know when to use SE16H, when to run ACDOCA separately, and when to use SAP-released CDS content instead.

 

Real-World Business Case

A Finance user posts an expense journal. The document posts successfully and the amounts are correct, but a reporting user later reports that the profit center shown in the Universal Journal does not match what they expected from the original entry. The support team needs to answer four questions quickly:

  1. Who created the document, on what date, in which currency, and through which transaction?
  2. What did the operational accounting document contain at entry-view level?
  3. What account assignment reached the Universal Journal for the leading ledger?
  4. Is the difference a true derivation issue, a document-splitting/ledger representation issue, or simply a misunderstanding of entry view versus Universal Journal view?

What Each Table Contributes

Table

Role in the investigation

Typical fields to expose

BKPF

Accounting document header

BUKRS, BELNR, GJAHR, BLART, BLDAT, BUDAT, WAERS, XBLNR, BKTXT, USNAM, TCODE

BSEG

BUZEI, BSCHL, KOART, SHKZG, HKONT, WRBTR, DMBTR, KOSTL, PRCTR, ZUONR, SGTXT

ACDOCA

Universal Journal line items / ledger representation

RLDNR, RBUKRS, GJAHR, BELNR, DOCLN, RACCT, RCNTR, PRCTR, SEGMENT, TSL/HSL and relevant currency fields

Why this combination is useful

SAP itself provides a released operational journal-entry CDS view that combines journal-entry item data from ACDOCA with operational accounting-document item data from BSEG and header data from BKPF. That is strong evidence that these three sources answer complementary Finance questions. For an ad hoc support exercise, SE16H lets us explore the same three layers interactively.

 

Join Architecture Used in This Guide

We will build the query in two stages:

  1. Create a dependable BSEG + BKPF relationship using the accounting-document key.
  2. Add ACDOCA at document level and restrict it to the relevant ledger for Universal Journal comparison.

Do not join on BELNR alone

Accounting document numbers can repeat across company codes and fiscal years. Always carry Company Code + Accounting Document + Fiscal Year together. Where the join-maintenance screen requires or exposes client handling, keep client consistency as well.

Why we do not join BUZEI directly to DOCLN

BSEG item number and ACDOCA Universal Journal line number do not represent a universally guaranteed one-to-one mapping. Ledger-specific lines, document splitting, technical postings, and other S/4HANA behavior can change the Universal Journal granularity. This guide therefore uses ACDOCA for controlled document-level analysis and explains row multiplication explicitly.

 

Prerequisites and Safety

  • Use a sandbox or non-production system for learning.
  • You need authorization to execute SE16H and read BKPF, BSEG, and ACDOCA.
  • If you cannot create or save an Outer Join Definition, ask your Basis/security team whether join-maintenance authorization is restricted.
  • Start with one known accounting document rather than a broad date range.
  • Do not use the three-table result as an aggregation or reconciliation total until you have confirmed row cardinality.
  • Avoid running unrestricted BSEG/ACDOCA selections in a large productive system.
  • Your screen labels can differ slightly by S/4HANA release and support package.

 

Step-by-Step: Build the SE16H Join

Step 1 - Launch SE16H

Run transaction SE16H. The initial screen contains the main table field and additional options such as database connection, output controls, grouping/aggregation options, and Outer Join Definition.

 

Step 2 - Enter BSEG as the primary table

Enter BSEG in the Table field. We start with BSEG because the support question begins at operational accounting-document line-item level.

Table = BSEG

 

Step 3 - Identify the document key

Create a descriptive definition. Example:

Join Definition: ZFI_BSEG_BKPF_ACDOCA

Description: FI Document - Entry View and Universal Journal

Naming tip

Use a descriptive Z* name in a sandbox if your system permits it. Your organization may have a different naming convention or may restrict saving join definitions.

 

Step 6 - Add BKPF as the first secondary table

Add BKPF as a secondary table. The relationship is one accounting header to one or more BSEG items.

Step 8 - Select useful BKPF output fields

Do not output every BKPF column. For troubleshooting, start with:

  • BLART - Document Type

Now add ACDOCA so that the same document can be examined in the Universal Journal.

Secondary table = ACDOCA

Do not add DOCLN = BUZEI by default

The tutorial intentionally does not define ACDOCA-DOCLN = BSEG-BUZEI. If you need a true item-level combined semantic model, use a SAP-released CDS view such as I_JournalEntryOperationalView or verify the mapping for your exact process first.

 

Step 11 - Restrict ACDOCA to the relevant ledger - only is required

For a leading-ledger investigation, apply a filter such as:

ACDOCA-RLDNR = '0L'

Use the ledger that is actually relevant in your system. Do not assume 0L if your business question is about a different ledger. This filter is required only if you want to restrict leading ledger entries in join condition. for this exercise we will extract entries for all ledgers. 

 

Step 12 - Choose ACDOCA output fields

For the profit-center troubleshooting case, select a focused set:

  • RLDNR - Ledger
  • DOCLN - Universal Journal line number
  • RACCT - G/L Account
  • RCNTR - Cost Center
  • PRCTR - Profit Center
  • SEGMENT - Segment
  • HSL / TSL or other relevant amount fields
  • Relevant currency-type/currency fields available in your release

 

Step 13 - Save and select the join definition

Save the join definition and return to the SE16H selection screen. Confirm that the definition is selected.

 

Step 14 - Enter the accounting-document selection criteria

Restrict the query to the known document:

BSEG-BUKRS = 1710

BSEG-BELNR = 100001768

BSEG-GJAHR = 2026

 

Step 15 - Select the primary BSEG fields

Recommended BSEG output for this business case:

  • BUZEI - Entry-view item
  • BSCHL - Posting Key
  • KOART - Account Type
  • SHKZG - Debit/Credit Indicator
  • HKONT - G/L Account
  • WRBTR - Document Currency Amount
  • DMBTR - Local Currency Amount
  • KOSTL - Cost Center
  • PRCTR - Profit Center
  • ZUONR - Assignment
  • SGTXT - Item Text

 

Step 16 - Execute the query

Execute the selection. The result should contain fields from all three sources: BSEG operational items, BKPF header information, and ACDOCA Universal Journal information.

 

Understand the Result Before Interpreting It

Why the same BSEG item can appear more than once

This is the most important concept in a three-table SE16H query. BKPF is effectively one header for the document, but both BSEG and ACDOCA can contain multiple rows. When BSEG and ACDOCA are connected only at document level, every matching BSEG row can be paired with multiple matching ACDOCA rows.

Example:

BSEG contains 2 items

ACDOCA (ledger 0L) contains 2 items

Document-level join can return up to 2 x 2 = 4 combinations for 0L ledger and 4 lines for 2L ledger

This is not a system error

Repeated rows in this query can be a natural consequence of joining two one-to-many data sets under the same document header. The result is useful for inspection and comparison, but you must not total the amounts as if each output row were a unique accounting line.

 

Analyze the Business Case

Now answer the original support question in layers.

Confirm document context from BKPF

  • BLART: Was this the expected document type?
  • BUDAT: Was it posted in the expected period?
  • WAERS: Is the transaction currency what the user expected?
  • TCODE: Was the document created through FB50 or another process?
  • USNAM: Which user or technical user created the document?

 

Check the entry-view assignment in BSEG

  • Which BSEG item represents the expense line?
  • What G/L account is in HKONT?
  • What Cost Center is present in KOSTL?
  • What Profit Center is present in PRCTR, if populated?
  • Does the amount match what is displayed in FB03?

 

Check the Universal Journal representation in ACDOCA

  • Which ledger is the line in (RLDNR)?
  • Which Universal Journal G/L account is in RACCT?
  • What Cost Center is represented in RCNTR?
  • What Profit Center is represented in PRCTR?
  • Is SEGMENT populated?
  • Are there more Universal Journal lines than operational BSEG items?

 

Example interpretation

Suppose the expense line in BSEG shows Cost Center CC4100 and Profit Center PC1000, while the ACDOCA result contains PC1000 on the original line plus additional Universal Journal lines created by ledger processing or document splitting. In that case, the user may not be looking at a simple one-line-to-one-line transformation. The investigation should move toward derivation/document-splitting logic rather than assuming that BSEG and ACDOCA must have identical item counts.

 

What to Compare in a Finance Support Ticket

Do not assume one-to-one without validation

Understand currency basis before comparing

 

Useful SE16H Features to Add to the Blog

Group

SE16H can group results for quick counts and distribution checks. For example, you can group by BLART, company code, G/L account, or profit center depending on the analysis.

Total and aggregation

For single-table or carefully designed queries, SE16H can total or aggregate numeric fields. However, do not total amounts in the document-level three-table query described above unless you have removed duplicate combinations and confirmed cardinality.

Aggregation warning

A document-level BSEG + ACDOCA join can multiply rows. Totals from that result can therefore be overstated. Use standalone BSEG/ACDOCA selections or a semantically correct CDS/report for reconciliation totals.

Sort and sequence

Use sequence/sort options to arrange the output in a logical order, for example Document → BSEG Item → ACDOCA DOCLN. This makes repeated combinations much easier to see.

 

Troubleshooting the SE16H Join

Symptom

Likely cause

What to check

No result

Wrong company code/year/document or ledger filter

Validate the document first in FB03, then test each table separately.

Too many rows

BSEG and ACDOCA both have multiple items

Expected document-level multiplication; filter ledger and validate tables separately.

Wrong header appears

Join too broad

Confirm BUKRS + BELNR + GJAHR; do not use BELNR alone.

ACDOCA fields blank

No matching row under current filters / join type

Check RBUKRS, BELNR, GJAHR and RLDNR in standalone ACDOCA.

Cannot create join definition

Authorization or system restriction

Check security/Basis policy; use temporary analysis or an approved reporting tool.

Performance is poor

Selection too broad / too many output fields

Restrict document/company/year early; reduce fields; avoid large ad hoc joins.

Amounts appear duplicated

Row multiplication

Do not total the three-table result; use a clean source for totals.

 

When SE16H Is the Right Tool - and When It Is Not

Good use cases

  • Targeted support analysis of one or a small number of documents.
  • Understanding how header, entry-view, and Universal Journal fields relate.
  • Quick proof-of-concept checks before designing a formal report.
  • Learning and troubleshooting in a sandbox.
  • Checking whether a value exists in one layer but not another.

Use another approach when

  • You need production-grade reporting over large volumes.
  • You require guaranteed item-level semantics between ACDOCA and BSEG.
  • You are building reconciliation totals or audit evidence.
  • You need a reusable governed data model for analytics.
  • Your organization requires released APIs/CDS views instead of direct table access.

SAP-released alternative

For a semantically defined combined operational journal-entry view, SAP provides I_JournalEntryOperationalView, which exposes ACDOCA journal-entry item details together with corresponding BSEG operational-item details and BKPF header details. For formal development/reporting, this is often safer than inventing a line-level table join.

Conclusion

For me, the main takeaway is that an FI posting should not be looked at only from the transaction screen. Understanding what happens in the background and how the data is stored in BKPF, BSEG, and ACDOCA makes troubleshooting much easier.

This is especially useful for functional consultants because it helps connect the business process with the technical side of SAP. Tools like SE16H can also help validate the posting and understand the data flow when something does not look right.

I hope this article gives a practical starting point for anyone who wants to understand SAP FI postings beyond just the configuration and transaction screens.

entry.title: When AI Meets SAP Integration: Exploring the New Possibilities of API Management
entry.content:
Imagine asking an AI assistant a simple business question:

“Can you check where my order is and tell me whether it will arrive tomorrow?”

For a person, this sounds like a straightforward request. But behind that one question, several things might need to happen. The assistant may need to retrieve the order from SAP, check delivery information, contact a logistics service, and combine the results before responding.

For an enterprise, this is where things get interesting.

The challenge is no longer just connecting one system to another. It is making business capabilities available to AI applications without losing control over security, access, and governance.

This is one of the areas where SAP Integration Suite is evolving, particularly through API Management, API-centric integration, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) support.

As someone working with SAP integration scenarios, I find this an interesting direction because it raises a practical question: How can we make the APIs and integration capabilities enterprises already have useful to AI applications?

From connecting systems to enabling AI

For years, integration development has focused on connecting applications, transforming payloads, routing messages, and ensuring that business data reaches the right destination.

A typical integration might retrieve a file from SFTP, transform CSV data into XML, and deliver the result to an SAP-related system. Another might expose an API that retrieves customer or delivery information.

These patterns remain important. But when an AI assistant enters the picture, there is another requirement: the assistant needs a structured and controlled way to discover and use the capabilities that already exist.

An AI agent should not simply have unrestricted access to every backend system. It needs access to the right operations, with appropriate permissions and safeguards.

This is where API Management becomes more than a place to manage API traffic. It can help establish the controls around how enterprise capabilities are exposed and consumed.

Where does MCP fit into this picture?

One concept worth understanding is the Model Context Protocol, or MCP.

MCP provides a standardized way for compatible AI applications to discover and interact with tools and resources. Instead of building a separate, custom connection for every AI application and every backend capability, developers can expose selected operations through an MCP-compatible interface.

Let's return to our delivery-status example.

The organization already has an API that retrieves delivery information. It may also have an API that retrieves order details. The business logic does not necessarily need to be rebuilt just because an AI assistant is introduced.

Instead, selected capabilities can be made available to an AI agent through a suitable MCP-based architecture.

The agent can discover an available tool, provide the required input, and use the returned result to answer the user's question.

MCP does not replace the underlying APIs. It provides a standardized way for AI applications to interact with capabilities exposed through compatible MCP servers.

Bringing the pieces together

This is where SAP Integration Suite's MCP Gateway becomes relevant. It provides a way to govern access to MCP-based capabilities, helping connect AI consumers with enterprise services through a managed entry point.

Consider the following conceptual architecture.

                  Business User
                       |
                       v
                 AI Assistant
                       |
                       v
                    MCP Client
                       |
                       v
              +--------------------+
              | SAP Integration    |
              | Suite              |
              |                    |
              |     MCP Gateway    |
              |                    |
              | Authentication     |
              | Access Governance  |
              | Traffic Controls   |
              +--------------------+
                       |
                 +-----+-----+
                 |           |
                 v           v
           SAP Business   Logistics
                API          API
                 |           |
                 v           v
             SAP S/4HANA   Tracking System
                 |           |
                 +-----+-----+
                       |
                       v
             Delivery Information
                       |
                       v
                 AI Assistant
                       |
                       v
             Response to the User

Figure: A conceptual architecture showing how an AI assistant could access selected SAP and third-party business capabilities through a governed MCP entry point.

The important point is not the number of components in the diagram. It is the separation of responsibilities.

The business APIs continue to provide the underlying operations. The MCP interface enables compatible AI applications to discover and invoke selected tools. The gateway provides a place to apply appropriate governance and traffic controls.

This is particularly useful to consider in enterprise landscapes, where one business process can span multiple applications, APIs, and security boundaries.

The exact architecture will depend on the available services, the MCP client, authentication requirements, and the capabilities supported by the organization's SAP Integration Suite environment.

API Management is also getting smarter

The AI story does not stop at exposing APIs to AI agents. AI can also help developers and administrators understand the APIs they already manage.

SAP API Management provides an AI-assisted analytics experience that allows users to explore API usage and performance through natural-language questions.

Think about a developer investigating an API that has suddenly started receiving more requests than usual. Rather than beginning with several filters and dashboard views, the developer could use a natural-language question to explore the available analytics.

Questions about request volumes, API performance, or consumer activity can become a more accessible starting point for investigation.

The generated insights still need to be checked against the underlying data, but this approach can make API analytics easier to explore.

For integration teams, that is an interesting shift: AI can become both a consumer of governed enterprise services and an assistant for people managing those services.

What is changing in SAP's integration landscape?

SAP's direction combines several related ideas.

API-centric integration brings API design, mediation, and governance closer together. MCP Gateway addresses the need to govern access to capabilities used by compatible AI applications. AI-assisted API analytics helps users explore API activity more naturally.

These capabilities solve different problems, but they point toward a common goal: making enterprise integration assets easier to expose, understand, and consume.

SAP's MCP support is also evolving. Its October 2026 release documentation describes support for MCP specification version 2026-07-28 and an increase in the maximum number of tools configurable on a single MCP server from 30 to 50.

These details matter when designing an implementation, but the bigger story is how standardized AI-to-tool communication can fit into an enterprise integration strategy.

As always, actual availability depends on the service, region, and tenant configuration, so the relevant SAP documentation should be checked before adopting a feature.

What does this mean for integration developers?

For developers who already work with SAP Cloud Integration, this is an extension of the integration landscape rather than a reason to abandon existing skills.

Payload transformation, connectivity, orchestration, security, and error handling remain fundamental. What changes is how some of the capabilities built on top of these foundations may be discovered and consumed.

An integration flow that retrieves or transforms business information may remain part of the solution. An API may provide access to that information. An MCP-based interface can then make a selected capability available to a compatible AI agent, with governance applied at the appropriate points.

Of course, not every integration needs AI. A scheduled file transfer or a straightforward system-to-system interface should not automatically become an AI use case.

The opportunity is to identify scenarios where natural-language interaction or agent-driven tool use adds real value, then expose only the capabilities needed for that scenario.

For me, that is the most useful way to think about these developments: the goal is not to add AI to every integration, but to make the right enterprise capabilities safely accessible when AI can genuinely help.

Closing thoughts

Enterprise integration is moving beyond the question of how systems exchange data. It is also becoming a question of how applications, people, and AI agents can access business capabilities in a controlled and meaningful way.

SAP Integration Suite's API Management developments, together with MCP support and AI-assisted analytics, are worth watching as this landscape evolves.

The underlying principles remain familiar: build clear interfaces, protect business data, govern access, and monitor how services are used. What is changing is the range of consumers that can make use of those services.

As AI becomes more integrated into enterprise workflows, the role of integration developers will continue to matter—not just in connecting systems, but in helping ensure that the capabilities behind those systems can be used responsibly.

entry.title: MCP or A2A in SAP CAP? Start with the responsibility you want to expose
entry.content:
With SAP TechEd 2026 underway, there is plenty to explore: Joule Studio, agent interoperability, AI gateways and persistent memory. One architecture decision deserves a closer look before we add another agent to the landscape.

When an existing CAP application needs to participate in an AI workflow, should we expose its capabilities through MCP, or turn a service into an agent available through A2A?

I would start by deciding who owns the reasoning. That makes the protocol choice much easier.

A tool request and a delegated task are different contracts

Take a hypothetical procurement application. A user wants to understand why an order is delayed.

“Read the latest delivery status for this order” is a bounded capability. The caller supplies an identifier, the service checks access and returns business data. The calling agent decides what to do with that result. MCP is a useful fit for exposing this kind of capability.

“Investigate this delay, compare the available options and bring back a recommendation” gives the receiving component more responsibility. It may need to choose tools, gather information over several steps and ask for missing input. That is the kind of delegation for which I would consider an agent interface through A2A.

The same business scenario can use both: one agent receives the task and calls tools to carry it out.

What CAP provides for Node.js

The CAP MCP adapter is installed with npm add @cap-js/mcp. An existing service can be exposed using annotate CatalogService with @McP;. It adds a protocol surface to the service; it does not, by itself, introduce an agent that reasons through a task.

There is also an easy naming trap here. @cap-js/mcp exposes application capabilities. @cap-js/mcp-server supports AI-assisted development of CAP projects. Choose according to whether the consumer needs business functionality or development assistance.

See the CAP MCP adapter guide.

For an agent, CAP documents npm add @cap-js/agents and the @AGent annotation. The plugin provides a reasoning-and-action loop over service tools and exposes the agent through A2A. That changes the behavior you are operating: the component now makes choices about how to use those tools.

CAP Node.js also supports @AGent.hitl on actions. When the agent selects such an action, the task pauses for human approval. This is useful for consequential actions, but it should sit alongside backend authorization and business validation.

See the CAP-level agents guide.

Keep the business rules in the service

For the procurement example, I would keep status lookup read-only and expose only the fields needed for the investigation. A separate action could submit an approved change, with its own permissions and validation.

CAP provides @requires, @restrict and instance-based access controls. @readonly limits operations on an entity; it does not decide which user's records someone may read. Model both the allowed operation and the allowed data scope.

Test that scope with different identities. A successful local call using a mock user does not demonstrate that the deployed identity flow is correct.

See CAP-level authorization.

Test the responsibility you added

For an MCP capability, I would test the input contract, access restrictions, query limits and returned fields.

For a delegated agent task, I would add cases that check its decisions: an ambiguous order reference, conflicting delivery information, a denied tool call, and a proposed change the user rejects. The result should explain what was found and what remains uncertain.

A deterministic lookup does not need another reasoning loop simply because the caller is an agent. Add one where the receiving service needs to make decisions and where you can evaluate those decisions.

Check release status before designing around it

CAP's September 2026 release notes mark the MCP adapter as generally available and introduce CAP-level agents under the Gamma label. Keep those statuses separate when assessing dependencies and support expectations. Recheck the release notes and plugin versions for your implementation.

Source: CAP September 2026 release notes.

SAP's October 27 TechEd announcement also highlights MCP and A2A interoperability and the new Enterprise AI Gateway. That makes this a timely design discussion, but an announcement does not establish that every capability is enabled in a particular tenant.

Source: SAP TechEd 2026 announcement.

For a first implementation, I would choose one business capability and make its responsibility clear. Does the consumer need a result from a tool, or does it need another agent to work through a task? That answer is a useful starting point for the architecture.

entry.title: Building an Agentic Harness Inside S/4HANA On-Premise with the ABAP AI SDK
entry.content:
@David150 @Dinis_Shubin 
An S/4HANA question rarely arrives with a table name, a complete key, and an agreed interpretation. Finding an answer can involve discovering a source, checking field meanings, and deciding what to investigate next. This project explores how an agentic harness, the application loop connecting a model to executable tools, can support that investigation from inside ABAP.
 
The agent answers user questions in natural language about the configuration of the underlying S/4HANA on-premise system. By connecting established SAP landscapes to modern language models, it brings older S/4HANA on-premise systems into the AI era.
Users can interact with the agent via a web interface. Find out exactly how that works here: Following a Conversation from the Browser into ABAP and Back .
 
The language model, gpt-5.6-sol, is deployed on the AI Core. The harness connects through the ABAP AI SDK's completion API using an Intelligent Scenario. ABAP owns the conversation state, tool execution, and repeated calls that turn a single completion into an investigation.
 
 
The research agent retains conversation context and a fresh writer reviews each completed turn.

The SDK provides message containers and function registration. The harness describes each tool's purpose and parameters, using ABAP runtime type information to define parameter types. The research agent exposes five capabilities: generated ABAP execution and four reads into the reusable Open Knowledge Format (OKF) system map. Tool descriptions become part of the interface through which the model plans its next step. You can find out more about how our OKF implementation works here: Hosting Open Knowledge Format Inside S/4HANA On-Premise with Z Tables .

The harness requests a completion using the current conversation. If the response contains tool calls, the dispatcher checks their names against the registered catalog and extracts their arguments. Each result is attached to its corresponding call and added to the conversation. The next model call can use that evidence to investigate further. A response without tool calls ends the normal loop.


Tool results, scanner rejections, and execution diagnostics all feed the next decision.

For example, a question about a configuration source can lead to a focused Dictionary query, followed by another query using the discovered fields and keys. Generated code supplies only the body of an existing FORM, assigning its result to a predefined string variable. The execution helper compiles the wrapped source with GENERATE SUBROUTINE POOL in a separate synchronous RFC session using DESTINATION 'NONE'. Compilation and caught runtime errors return as feedback, allowing another attempt.

That flexibility brings ordinary application responsibilities into agent design. The research agent can only perform read-only tasks on S/4 business data and configuration. Restricted execution is enabled by default: a scanner using SCAN ABAP-SOURCE checks generated statements, rejecting database writes and unapproved calls before execution. It permits SELECT SINGLE while other SELECT queries require a literal row limit between 1 and 1,000. These checks filter operations. Business data authorization and total workload require their own controls. A loop-counter cap of 25 triggers one forced completion call.

Reusing one controller per conversation preserves the research agent's context across questions. After each completed turn, the controller starts a fresh asynchronous writer to review reusable findings and maintain OKF. This gives answering questions and curating knowledge separate objectives and tool catalogs.

The central engineering lesson is that an agent needs an explicit execution contract. The model proposes investigation steps, the harness controls dispatch, preserves state, returns evidence, and limits repetition. The SDK supplies the connection to the model, while those application decisions shape how reliably the investigation proceeds.

entry.title: Hosting Open Knowledge Format Inside S/4HANA On-Premise with Z Tables
entry.content:
@David150 @Dinis_Shubin 
A brand-new knowledge format and an older S/4HANA on-premise system can seem an unlikely pairing. Yet S/4HANA already provides much of what agent-maintained knowledge needs: structured persistence, client separation, authorization checks, and reliable transactions. In this project, custom Z tables turn Open Knowledge Format (OKF) into a reusable map of the system the agent investigates.
 
First of all: If you haven't already read our main blogpost about the S/4HANA On-Premise agent that we built, you can do so here: Building an Agentic Harness Inside S/4HANA On-Premise with the ABAP AI SDK 
 
OKF represents knowledge as Markdown documents with YAML metadata, organized into bundles. Each concept describes one asset or meaning; tags classify it, links connect it, and a directory supports navigation. Version 0.2 adds optional provenance, verification, lifecycle, and computation contracts. It prescribes an exchange format without prescribing a database or runtime. That leaves room for an ABAP-managed working representation.

The storage model uses four client-dependent tables. Bundle records hold descriptive metadata, a Markdown navigation directory, the format version, and timestamps. Concept records hold a path-like identity, type, title, summary, Markdown body, lifecycle status, and creation, change, and verification times. Separate tables hold tags and directed relationships, including readable relationship labels.
 

 

Markdown carries the explanation while relational records support navigation and maintenance.
 
This is a knowledge graph built from ordinary relational structures. A configuration source can connect to a business meaning through an explicit relationship. Tags offer another route across domains. Keeping these connections separately makes them searchable and editable without parsing every document body.

The research agent lists bundles, opens a directory, searches relevant concepts, and loads selected bodies with incoming and outgoing relationships. Search supports literal keywords, type, tag, hierarchy prefix, and lifecycle filters, with cursor-based pagination. This progressive disclosure keeps the agent focused on relevant knowledge.

After a completed conversation turn, a fresh asynchronous writer reviews the findings and checks existing knowledge for duplicates. Its instructions require direct, current, read-only evidence for material facts. It preserves source locations, keys, meanings, and retrieval contracts. Actual configuration values and business results remain live reads. The graph remembers how to find and interpret them.

Verification and lifecycle answer different questions. A concept can be draft, stable, or deprecated. Stable is the default search scope, while verification is recorded separately. Finalization timestamps explicit concept changes on the writer's assertion of verification. That timestamp records confirmation. However it neither expires automatically nor guarantees continuing accuracy.
 
 
Writes first accumulate in memory. Finalization checks authorizations and inputs, conditionally locks affected bundle revisions in a consistent order, validates references, and prepares one write plan. Concepts, tags, relationships, and directory updates then commit together. A failure rolls back database changes and discards staging.

Each writer must supply the bundle revision it read. If another writer commits first, the outdated proposal is rejected. The writer reloads, reassesses, and stages the complete change again. This protects against lost updates when asynchronous investigations overlap, provided every writer follows the same service protocol.

Retirement preserves the concept and its relationships for historical navigation. A replacement can be linked, misleading tags or relationships removed, and the directory adjusted in the same transaction. Direct retrieval still exposes retired knowledge with its status.

The current representation implements a focused subset. Portable bundle export, multiple verifier identities, and per-run computation attestation remain outside the current implementation. Those are distinct from storing readable knowledge and recording a verification time.

An older S/4HANA system is a capable host for modern knowledge management. Its Dictionary supplies evidence close to the source, while ABAP authorization checks and database transactions give agent-driven curation an established operational foundation.

entry.title: Following a Conversation from the Browser into ABAP and Back
entry.content:
@Dinis_Shubin @David150 

The first post, about building an agentic harness inside S/4HANA On-premise with the ABAP AI SDK, explained the ABAP AI SDK's model-and-tool loop. Here, we follow its request and response contract, then examine how a WebSocket keeps successive questions connected to the agent's conversation context.

The request and response contract

The application backend sends each question to SAP as a JSON text frame over WebSocket Secure (WSS):

{ "type": "prompt", "prompt": "Which assignments did you check?" }

SAP validates the prompt, reserves the connection's single active request, and returns an accepted frame with a fresh correlation_id. That acknowledges admission. Model and tool events follow. A representative terminal answer has this shape:

{
  "outcome": "ok",
  "response_type": "final_response",
  "is_final": true,
  "correlation_id": "0123456789ABCDEF0123456789ABCDEF",
  "step": 3,
  "content": "The complete answer."
}
Field Meaning
outcomeaccepted admits the request. progress carries intermediate events. ok completes a successful answer.
response_typeIdentifies tool_call, tool_response, context_compaction, or final_response.
is_finalEnds the request when true. A final_response chunk can still be non-terminal.
correlation_idIdentifies one request and its replay records. Every question gets a new ID.
stepOrders public events within that request. It does not count model iterations or tokens.

The backend accumulates only final_response content into the answer and keeps tool details separate. It maps SAP events to the browser's server-sent events (SSE), including answer-delta and complete. The browser therefore does not hold the SAP WebSocket or SAP credentials.

 

 

Why execution and delivery need separate sessions

ABAP Push Channels (APC) handle the WebSocket. The request callback establishes a request-filtered output binding, starts asynchronous processing, and returns. It does not execute the investigation itself.

The conversation worker and output relay run in separate ABAP internal sessions. A synchronous SDK or tool call occupies the worker's execution path. The relay must remain available to receive and deliver events. Its subscription starts before agent work, preventing a fast response from arriving before a receiver exists.

The agent publishes ABAP Messaging Channels (AMC) events as Push Channel Protocol (PCP) messages. The relay's receiver queues them. Normal code drains that queue after WAIT FOR MESSAGING CHANNELS returns, because persistence requires COMMIT WORK, which cannot run inside the receiver callback.

The publisher checks request identity, event type, content bounds, and finality. It assigns the public step, persists and commits the frame, then publishes request-filtered AMC text onto the APC binding. This ordering makes output available for replay before live notification.

Who owns the message container?

The APC handler is stateless across callbacks. Conversation memory belongs to the retained agent inside the worker's internal session.

SAP resolves the original handshake's Sec-WebSocket-Key to a private worker key, with independent SAP user/client checks. The registry stores lifecycle metadata, not serialized agent state. The handshake key provides routing, not authorization.

On the first turn, the worker creates the agent, which creates its SDK message container and sets the system role. Each turn appends the user message, tool interactions and results, and the assistant's answer. The next completion receives that context. Without the earlier assistant answer, a follow-up such as “Which assignments did you check?” would lack the answer it refers to.

Conversation ownership.

A later question uses the same physical SAP WebSocket. A new request relay subscribes, then dispatches the turn through a private AMC command channel to the existing worker. The output binding and correlation ID change. The retained agent context continues. Overlapping SAP requests are rejected before they can replace the active binding.

An application conversation ID selects the socket in the backend. It is not sent to SAP as a conversation identifier. The SDK container is an ABAP object. Its reference stays inside the owning session.

Connection loss and context changes

Browser SSE delivery can reconnect while the backend's SAP socket remains live. SAP WebSocket reconnect is different: the protocol can replay one request's output using its correlation ID, but future prompts on the replacement socket start fresh context. Replay can duplicate steps. Clients must deduplicate by correlation ID and step. The current backend reports upstream conversation loss rather than automatically performing SAP replay.

Worker memory expires after approximately 15 idle minutes, even if the socket stays open. Keepalive pings maintain transport connectivity. They are not conversation turns. The current close callback leaves worker cleanup to idle expiry.

During a live conversation, context compaction can summarize older history and replace the SDK container inside the same agent. Conversation continuity therefore depends on retained context, not permanent object identity.

The protocol accepts answer chunks, but the current agent uses synchronous completion and emits its completed answer as one terminal event. Investigation progress can arrive earlier. This does not imply token-by-token model streaming. If the user stops waiting after SAP receives a prompt, the backend still drains that request to its terminal event to preserve socket ordering.
